result:
The proposed answer of 2 is incorrect, because the counterexample it relies on does not work.

The ideal I = (x, y², z) is a monomial complete intersection. Its generators form a regular sequence, so it is normal, and in particular it is not a counterexample. The claim that y² ∈ Ī² \ I² is also unfounded, since y² is itself a generator of I and has no bearing on I². The ideal I is not even integrally closed, because y lies in its integral closure but not in I. So the "N = 3 fails" step collapses.

The vacuous-truth argument for N ≤ 2 is also not a valid way to find the maximum. A height-3 monomial ideal needs at least 3 generators, and every integrally closed ideal with exactly 3 generators here is normal, so the true maximum is at least 3.

I did not derive the true value of N here. From memory, the known result is that integrally closed monomial ideals of height 3 in k[x,y,z] with few generators are normal, with a non-normal example appearing at a larger generator count. That would put N well above 2.

VERDICT: REJECT
